set_title: Chest pain: which coronary syndrome, or the aorta
stem: A 60-year-old man has had 8 months of substernal pressure when he climbs two flights of stairs, resolving within 5 minutes of rest. He has had no pain at rest. Troponin I is normal.
oneliner: 60M + 8 months of substernal pressure on stairs + gone within 5 min of rest + no rest pain + normal troponin → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Prinzmetal angina strikes **at rest, often at night**; his pain comes only on stairs
whyNot.B: MI gives prolonged pain with a raised troponin; his pain **clears within 5 minutes and troponin I is normal**
whyNot.D: Dissection causes abrupt, severe pain that persists; his pain is **repeatable on stairs for 8 months and clears with rest**
whyNot.E: Unstable angina brings pain **at rest** or at a falling threshold; he has none at rest

why: Pressure that appears at a fixed workload and **goes away with rest, with a normal troponin**, fits a fixed coronary stenosis causing demand ischemia without plaque rupture or necrosis.

set_title: Chest pain: which coronary syndrome, or the aorta
stem: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history has sudden, severe chest pain with sweating and nausea. Pulse is 110/min. ECG shows ST elevation in the inferior leads. Myocardial infarction is suspected, but aortic dissection is also being considered.
oneliner: 58M + hypertension + smoker + sudden severe chest pain + sweating and nausea + pulse 110 + inferior ST elevation → MI or dissection?
ask: Which single finding favours aortic dissection over myocardial infarction?

options.C: ST elevation in the inferior leads
options.E: A 25 mm Hg arm-to-arm pressure difference

whyNot.A: **Sweating and nausea** occur in both
whyNot.B: **A pulse of 110/min** fits both
whyNot.C: **Inferior ST elevation** occurs in both, because a dissection can tear across the right coronary ostium
whyNot.D: **Hypertension and smoking** raise the risk of both

answer: A 25 mm Hg arm-to-arm pressure difference
why: The tear narrows or occludes the origin of a branch, so a **blood-pressure difference between the arms** (or a new aortic regurgitation murmur or wide mediastinum) points to dissection. Giving a fibrinolytic or anticoagulant after mistaking it for STEMI can be fatal.

set_title: Sharp chest pain after a virus: pericardium, myocardium, pleura or chest wall
stem: A 17-year-old boy has had 2 days of sharp substernal chest pain, 1 week after a febrile illness with a sore throat. Temperature is 37.9 C. A high-pitched scratching sound is heard at the left sternal border.
oneliner: 17M + sharp substernal pain + febrile illness 1 week ago + scratching sound at the left sternal border → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Costochondritis gives **tenderness at the costochondral junction** with a normal cardiac exam; he has a scratching sound
whyNot.C: Myocarditis presents with **dyspnea and a gallop**; his exam shows a scratching sound
whyNot.D: MI at 17 after a **febrile illness** with a scratching sound is unlikely; the sound is a rub, not an S4 or murmur
whyNot.E: Pleurodynia causes **chest-wall muscle pain without a rub**; he has a scratching sound at the sternal border

why: A **pericardial friction rub** after a viral illness (often coxsackie B) is pericarditis: inflamed visceral and parietal layers rub together in systole and diastole.

oneliner: 45M + 6 h severe chest pain + sweating + ST elevation V2-V5 + mildly raised troponin → pericarditis or MI?
ask: Which single finding favours acute pericarditis over myocardial infarction?

options.B: ST elevation in the precordial leads
options.E: PR-segment depression in the same leads

whyNot.A: **A raised troponin** occurs in both, because the epicardial myocardium is inflamed in pericarditis
whyNot.B: **Precordial ST elevation** is seen in anterior MI too

whyNot.D: **Sweating** accompanies both

why: Pericarditis lifts ST segments diffusely, in a concave pattern across territories, with **PR-segment depression**. MI gives convex regional ST elevation with reciprocal depression and later Q waves.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a 30-pack-year smoking history has hypertension that is now resistant to three drugs. A bruit is heard over the left flank. Renal angiography shows eccentric narrowing at the origin of the left renal artery.
oneliner: 52F + 30-pack-year smoker + resistant hypertension + flank bruit + eccentric narrowing at the renal artery origin → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Primary aldosteronism has **no bruit and no arterial lesion**; she has both
whyNot.B: Essential hypertension does not cause a **flank bruit or a renal artery lesion**
whyNot.C: Fibromuscular dysplasia gives **beading of the mid to distal artery**; hers is eccentric narrowing at the origin
whyNot.E: Pheochromocytoma causes **episodic** symptoms and no arterial narrowing; she has a bruit and a lesion

why: An **eccentric plaque at the origin or proximal renal artery**, a flank bruit and resistant hypertension in a smoker mean renovascular hypertension: the ischemic kidney secretes renin and raises angiotensin II and aldosterone.

stem: A 48-year-old man has blood pressure of 158/98 mm Hg on three visits. Serum sodium is 141 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, and creatinine is normal. He has no edema. Essential hypertension and primary aldosteronism are both being considered.
oneliner: 48M + BP 158/98 on three visits + Na 141 + K 4.1 + normal creatinine + no edema → essential hypertension or primary aldosteronism?
ask: Which single finding favours essential hypertension over primary aldosteronism?

options.A: Blood pressure above 140/90 on three visits

whyNot.A: **Sustained elevation** defines hypertension and does not point to a cause
whyNot.B: **A sodium of 141** is normal or high-normal in both; aldosterone escape stops it rising further
whyNot.C: **Normal creatinine** fits both
whyNot.E: **No edema** fits both; aldosterone escape (pressure natriuresis) prevents edema in primary aldosteronism

why: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest secondary cause, and most patients have a normal potassium, so a potassium of 4.1 does not exclude it. **A normal aldosterone-to-renin ratio** (no autonomous aldosterone with suppressed renin) does, leaving essential hypertension, a diagnosis of exclusion.
